newsitem.title: CANADA: Internet shell game; now you see it, now you don't.
newsitem.headline: Internet shell game; now you see it, now you don't.

text.p: It is only a month into the New Year and doom and gloom is swirling the Internet like a fierce winter storm.
Many believe the hype machine surrounding the World Wide Web is stalling and giving away to a more pessimistic outlook on what the future holds for the new digital frontier.

Even the Wall Street Journal weighed in with an in depth front page story on Jan. 14 detailing the many pullbacks and closures announced recently by content providers on the Web. "Facing Early Losses, Some Web Publishers Begin To Pull the Plug," read the headline.

As everyone well knows the dream of building exciting new Web sites has far outstripped the amount of advertising dollars available to support them. The sky really is the limit when thinking of the possibilities of developing a new medium that marries the intelligence of newspapers and magazines with the sights and sounds of television and radio.

But while many have tried to bring dreams to reality, mouths have been left gaping with the retrenchment of such popular sites as "The Spot," the Net soap opera by American Cybercast and the closure of the family-oriented "Wow!" online service by CompuServe.
Wired Ventures Inc. with its slick "Wired" magazine and other businesses seemed to personify the Net's problems last year with its on again and off again attempts to take its company public.

As the Los Angeles Times said in a December report about the Net: "It's the end of the beginning, the end of the very hyped, very heady first wave of the commercial Internet revolution. Next year reality bites the Internet business and bites hard..."
And ouch is the word. When talking with Internet executives there is a near palpable feeling in the air about their concern on what happens next on the Net.
One senior executive with a major software firm said he just laughs off any talk of attracting advertising to their Web pages because the prospects have become so bleak.
Indeed, Rick Broadhead, a co-author of the Canadian Internet Handbook, is seeing four major trends that could mean big changes on the Internet this year:
1. Integration of products and computers with the Internet; such as CD-ROM titles that come with Web connections for updates.
2. Push Technology; where services such as PointCast "push" news to the users rather than having the user go out and search for it.
3. Practical Internet Applications; where companies offer useful services, such as the Hallmark Cards site (http://wwwhallmark.com) which reminds users of important dates.
4. The shakeout; where some companies decide they cannot keep supporting money-losing sites.

Broadhead calls the shakeout a period of accountability for the Web. Perhaps for the next year we should picture the Internet as a desert of rapidly shifting sands ready to gobble up old players and presumably allowing others to come forth to rest on top for a while.
But is all this necessarily a bad thing? There has been a lot of talk of some high flying services backtracking for sure.

But one can be far more overwhelmed by all the new Web sites announced on the Net. The money that companies such as Microsoft and Sony are spending on the Web is mind boggling, not to mention the new sites being put up by banks, brokers, car companies and other retailers.

As well the Internet is all about change so why should we wring our hands over the occasional flops and resurrections. Expect fantastic pages to spring up and die almost as fast as they arrived. After all we don't like to get too bored out there.
So a short life for some worthy Web site should not be seen as a failure, but rather a brief shining moment in an always fascinating digital landscape.
